title: Ch-T-A
hookLine: chet, sin, means missing the mark, as slingers "not missing" (Judges 20:16)

lines: OFF THE FRONT OF THE RIM.
cards: Last seconds of a high-school game. A kid steps to the free-throw line, bounces the ball, breathes, shoots. It clangs off the front of the rim.
The gym goes quiet. Nobody calls it evil. Nobody says the kid is a bad person.
It's a miss, and the coach will say: bend your knees, follow through, again. Hold onto that gym. A Hebrew word for sin comes from a verb the Bible uses for exactly this.
Chet, tet, alef: Ch-T-A. To miss.

teach.b: Turn Ch-T-A four ways. First, the slingers. Judges describes left-handed fighters from the tribe of Benjamin who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
Not miss is lo yachati, from this very root. Before it's a moral word, it's a stone flying wide. Second, the noun.

teach.h: CHET: A STONE THAT FLIES WIDE.
teach.b: Chet is one of the Bible's words for sin, and you can hear the slingers inside it: an aim that went off, a target that was there, a stone that didn't reach it. Third, nobody is perfect.

teach.h: NOT A RIGHTEOUS MAN WHO SINNETH NOT.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes says it flatly: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." The verse doesn't say the target is fake, or that aim doesn't matter.
It says everyone who shoots will sometimes miss. Fourth, why we miss. Proverbs adds what anyone who's been late knows: the one who hurries with his feet misses, again Ch-T-A.
Speed, carelessness, a stone thrown without looking. Put it beside yesterday. If Torah is aiming, chet is the miss, and both belong to the same practice.
A miss is serious; someone can get hurt by a stone that goes wide. But a miss can also be studied.
Where did it go? Was I rushing? What would I adjust?
The coach at the free-throw line is already asking this root's question.

how: In the Yom Kippur liturgy Jews recite the Al Chet, a confession whose lines begin "for the sin," al chet, said together as a community.

o: a root for guilt, a stain that can't be washed out
a root for breaking a vow, as in a broken oath
a root for missing the mark, and so a word for sin

p: not a righteous man who sinneth not

s: the Hebrew word for sin grows from a verb for missing a target
Judges uses the root for slingers who aimed at a hair and did not miss.
Ecclesiastes says truly righteous people never sin
"there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not."
in Proverbs, hurrying is one way to miss
the one who hurries with his feet misses, from the same root.

games.q: Ecclesiastes is looking for a person on earth who does good and never misses. what does it find?
games.why: "there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." even the good miss sometimes.

practice: Bring to mind one small miss from the past few days, a sharp word, a promise that slipped, a moment you rushed past someone, and look at where the stone landed without arguing with it or punishing yourself.

Then ask the coach's questions: was I hurrying, what was I really aiming at, what one adjustment would bring the next shot closer? Hold that adjustment, and if you pray, bring the miss into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Ch-T-A. Chet, tet, alef: the root of chet, sin, from a verb for missing the mark, like a slinger's stone that goes wide. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: sin; from the root Ch-T-A, to miss the mark.

carryVoice: Your line: sin is missing the mark. Even the good miss. See you at the next one.

sources.q: For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.
